name: Utopian socialism
scope: The founding generation of utopian socialism as the defining sources name it: Saint-Simon, Fourier and Owen (Leopold, Britannica), with the later utopian communist Étienne Cabet and the communities and Owenite, Fourierist and Saint-Simonian movements they inspired; the label comes from Marx and Engels (Leopold, 'Marx, Engels, and Some (Non-Foundational) Arguments against Utopian Socialism'; Britannica 'utopian socialism'). Texts tied to it: Owen's A New View of Society, Fourier's Theory of the Four Movements, and Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific as the classic account. It excludes Marxism itself, later utopian fiction and the religious communitarian settlements Britannica mentions (Shakers, Mennonites, Mormons) except where they overlap; the three founders differ (Saint-Simon technocratic, Fourier on passions and association, Owen on education and circumstances).

alienated-labor.rationale: Britannica reports Fourier's charge that 'institutions such as marriage, the male-dominated family, and the competitive market confine people to repetitive labor or a limited role in life and thus frustrate the need for variety', and his remedy of 'attractive labor' in which each member moves among several occupations.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Leopold reports Owen's view that violence is counterproductive and ineffective, because a rational and humane society could not be brought about 'by violence, or through feelings of anger and ill-will to any portion of mankind', and that Owen sought a 'peaceful revolution' by communitarian example.

character-from-environment.rationale: Owen's first essay states: 'Any general character, from the best to the worst, from the most ignorant to the most enlightened, may be given to any community, even to the world at large, by the application of proper means'; Britannica gives his fundamental belief as that 'human nature is not fixed but formed' and that social conditions make people selfish or vicious.

class-collaboration.rationale: Leopold reports Owen's view that 'violence is based on an anger and ill-will towards other classes which is irrational', and that party strife is a 'desolating conflict between parties whose real interests are the same'; Owen held that the classes' interests are the same and that change comes by 'reason and kindness'.

collective-farming.rationale: Britannica describes Fourier's phalange as 'a cooperative agricultural community' and Cabet's Icaria as 'combining industry with farming' in one self-sufficient community.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Britannica on Owen's New Harmony: 'This was to be a self-sufficient, cooperative community in which property was commonly owned.' It describes Fourier's phalanstery as a self-sufficient community of about 1,600 people in which every member shares in ownership, and Cabet's Icaria as a self-sufficient community of common ownership.

death-penalty.rationale: Owen's A New View of Society objects that society forms 'such characters as they afterwards deem it a duty and a right to punish even to death'; Britannica gives his view that 'people are not a proper subject of either praise or blame'.

decide-locally.rationale: Britannica describes the founders' model as small self-sufficient communities (Owen's New Harmony, Fourier's phalanstery of about 1,600 people, Cabet's Icaria) and says Owen's ideas 'stimulated the formation of self-governing workshops'.

democracy-best.rationale: Leopold: 'He was famously uninterested in disputes over the form of the state; insisting that arguments about ‘despotism, aristocracy, and democracy’ were either irrelevant' (insofar as the cause of social problems was ignorance rather than who rules or how they are chosen), 'or part of the problem' (as a 'desolating conflict between parties whose real interests are the same').

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Leopold reports Owen's argument that 'violence is based on an anger and ill-will towards other classes which is irrational', and that party conflict is a 'desolating conflict between parties whose real interests are the same'.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Britannica's account differs between the founders: Fourier's phalanstery had 'inequality of wealth, though permitted, was to be limited', while Cabet's Icaria took up 'The ideas of common ownership, equality, and a simple life were taken up' in the novel Voyage en Icarie.

experts-over-public.rationale: Britannica gives Saint-Simon's argument that 'it makes sense to put the economic arrangements of society in the hands of its most knowledgeable and productive members'; his planners are 'scientists, industrialists, and engineers'.

gradual-change.rationale: Owen writes in A New View of Society that 'the smallest alteration, adequate to produce any good effect, should be made at one time; indeed, if possible, the change should be so gradual as to be almost imperceptible'.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Owen's first essay holds that 'Any general character, from the best to the worst, from the most ignorant to the most enlightened, may be given to any community, even to the world at large, by the application of proper means', and Britannica gives his belief that 'human nature is not fixed but formed'.

local-production.rationale: Britannica describes Owen's New Harmony as 'a self-sufficient, cooperative community', Fourier's phalanstery as 'a largely self-sufficient community' and Cabet's Icaria as 'a self-sufficient community, combining industry with farming'.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Owen holds that 'people are not a proper subject of either praise or blame' (Britannica) because character is formed by circumstances, and objects to society punishing characters it has formed itself (A New View of Society).

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Britannica says of Saint-Simon's planned system: 'Such a system would be more efficient than capitalism, according to Saint-Simon'; of Fourier it notes his emphasis on 'the wastefulness of the competitive capitalist system' and that the market 'frustrates the desire for harmony'.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Britannica says Fourier held that phalanges 'they could be introduced into any political system , including a monarchy', and Leopold reports Owen's view that arguments over 'despotism, aristocracy, and democracy' were irrelevant or part of the problem.

municipal-property.rationale: Britannica describes Owen's New Harmony as a community 'in which property was commonly owned' and Fourier's phalanstery as one in which 'every member was to share in ownership'.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Britannica reports Fourier's charge that the 'male-dominated family' confines people; Engels reports his criticism of 'the bourgeois form of the relations between sexes' and that 'the degree of woman’s emancipation is the natural measure of the general emancipation'.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Leopold reports Owen's three reasons against violence in 1849: it rests on 'anger and ill-will towards other classes which is irrational', it is counterproductive, and it is ineffective, since a rational and humane society could never be brought about 'by violence, or through feelings of anger and ill-will to any portion of mankind'.

production-for-use.rationale: Britannica reports Saint-Simon's scheme in which planners 'anticipate social needs and direct the energies of society to meet them', and Fourier's 'His emphasis on adapting society to human needs' against the wasteful competitive capitalist system.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Britannica reports that Owen concluded early that 'there were fundamental flaws in all religions' and, having 'lost all belief in the prevailing forms of religion', built his system on education; his 1849 book is titled 'The Coming Change from Irrationality to Rationality' (Leopold).

rehabilitation.rationale: Owen writes: 'Instead of punishing crimes after they have permitted the human character to be formed so as to commit them, they will adopt the only means which can be adopted to prevent the existence of those crimes'; Britannica adds that his New Lanark schools 'eschewed corporal punishment and other traditional methods' and 'emphasized character development'.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Britannica reports Fourier's charge: 'Modern society breeds selfishness, deception, and other evils', and notes that radicals were outraged by 'the self-interested competition of capitalists'.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Fourier names 'the Civilizees, in consequence of their tyranny over woman' as having failed to reach the sixth Period, and calls for the emancipation of women ('the emancipation of women and slaves, whose freedom is necessary to the organization of the Combined Order').

simple-living.rationale: Britannica: 'The ideas of common ownership, equality, and a simple life were taken up in the visionary novel Voyage en Icarie' by Étienne Cabet.

single-official-language.rationale: Fourier lists among the general results of association 'the establishment of Unities all over the globe, such as unity of language, unity of weights and measures, unity of typographic characters' (Theory of the Four Movements).

socialism-needs-revolutionary-war.rationale: Leopold reports Owen's view that violence is ineffective and that change comes 'by reason and kindness', and Fourier writes that association will end wars 'for ever, without the least violence'.

traditional-family.rationale: Britannica reports Fourier's charge that 'institutions such as marriage, the male-dominated family, and the competitive market' confine people to a limited role in life.

unions-good.rationale: Britannica says of Owen: 'His ideas influenced the growth of labor unionism', and that he led the trade union movement in the 1830s (the Grand National Consolidated Trades Union).

war-builds-character.rationale: Fourier writes in the Theory of the Four Movements that 'civilized nations are bathing themselves in blood in wars for commercial supremacy' while association will 'terminate these wars for ever, without the least violence'.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Fourier writes in the Theory of the Four Movements: 'freedom of divorce will be of great use in the sixth Period, and will contribute eminently toward domestic harmony'.

worker-ownership.rationale: Britannica credits Louis Blanc with a theory of worker-controlled “social workshops,” and says Owen 'he stimulated the formation of self-governing workshops'.

summary: Utopian socialism is the early 19th-century current, associated with Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen and Cabet, that condemned competitive industrial capitalism and proposed rationally planned, cooperative communities with shared property and attractive, varied labour. Owen held that character is formed by circumstances, so crime and vice are cured by education and environment rather than punishment; the school sought change by example and persuasion, peacefully and gradually, appealing to all classes rather than to class struggle.

notes: Searched themes: economy and ownership, labour, government and the state, society and family, crime and punishment, religion, women, ecology and settlement, culture, technology, means of change, world order. Answers rest on Britannica's articles on socialism, utopian socialism, Owen and Fourier, Leopold's chapter, Owen's A New View of Society and Fourier's Theory of the Four Movements. The founders differ (Saint-Simon on planning by experts, Fourier on unequal shares, Owen on common property), so where they do not agree the answer is a split or null. The Manifesto is a critic's account and answers nothing. The earlier pass's answers rested on dropped sources or readings of the founders' aims and were nulled where the defining sources do not state them.
